claim: Learning is shaped by prior knowledge, motivation, context, culture, metacognition, and opportunities for transfer.
citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. How People Learn II: Learners, Contexts, and Cultures.
why: Broad learning-science anchor for learner/context/system modeling and transfer.

claim: Design multiple means of engagement, representation, action, and expression while addressing barriers and exclusion.
citation: CAST. Universal Design for Learning Guidelines, Version 3.0.
why: Accessibility, learner agency, multiple representations, and barrier-aware design.

claim: Educational AI should keep humans in the loop, center learning goals, and attend to bias, safety, privacy, and evidence.
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Educational Technology. Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning: Insights and Recommendations.
why: Human-centered AI in education; governance and instructional use.

claim: Generative AI in education should be human-centered, age-appropriate, privacy-aware, ethically validated, and pedagogically designed.
citation: UNESCO. Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research.
why: Ethical/pedagogical guardrails for generative AI.

claim: AI risk management should be governed, mapped, measured, and managed across the system lifecycle.
citation: National Institute of Standards and Technology. Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0).
why: Risk, governance, measurement, and accountable deployment.

claim: Human-AI systems should set expectations, make uncertainty and controls visible, support correction, and preserve appropriate human agency.
citation: Amershi, S., et al. Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. CHI 2019.
why: Human-AI interaction design and calibrated reliance.

claim: Cognitive engagement can be distinguished as passive, active, constructive, and interactive, with different implications for learning.
citation: Chi, M. T. H., & Wylie, R. The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes.
why: Designing learner actions rather than optimizing superficial engagement.

claim: Across undergraduate STEM studies, active learning outperformed traditional lecture on achievement and failure outcomes.
citation: Freeman, S., et al. Active learning increases student performance in science, engineering, and mathematics. PNAS.
why: Evidence anchor for active practice and learner participation.

claim: Metacognition and self-regulation can be explicitly taught through planning, monitoring, evaluation, modeling, and scaffolded practice.
citation: Education Endowment Foundation. Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning, 2nd ed.
why: Metacognitive prompts, self-monitoring, and fading support.

claim: Feedback is most useful when it is connected to goals, task/process performance, and actionable next steps rather than person-level praise.
citation: Hattie, J., & Timperley, H. The Power of Feedback. Review of Educational Research.
why: Feedback design and evidence-producing practice.

claim: Multimedia can improve learning when words and visuals are designed around how people process information and unnecessary cognitive load is reduced.
citation: Mayer, R. E., & Fiorella, L. Introduction to Multimedia Learning, in The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, 3rd ed.
why: Multiple representations, multimedia, and cognitive-load-aware design.

claim: Transfer depends on what is learned and how similar or different the new context is across knowledge domain, physical/social context, time, and function.
citation: Barnett, S. M., & Ceci, S. J. When and where do we apply what we learn? A taxonomy for far transfer. Psychological Bulletin.
why: Transfer as a design and evaluation target.

claim: Simulation-based education with deliberate practice can outperform traditional clinical education for skill acquisition in studied contexts.
citation: McGaghie, W. C., et al. Does simulation-based medical education with deliberate practice yield better results than traditional clinical education? Academic Medicine.
why: Simulation, deliberate practice, and repeated performance with feedback.

claim: Effective support for English learners includes visual/verbal supports, peer interaction, monitoring progress, and use of home language and cultural assets.
citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Promoting the Educational Success of Children and Youth Learning English: Promising Futures.
why: Multilingual learner design and asset-based language support.

claim: Culturally sustaining pedagogy values and sustains linguistic, literate, and cultural pluralism rather than treating difference as a deficit.
citation: Paris, D. Culturally Sustaining Pedagogy: A Needed Change in Stance, Terminology, and Practice. Educational Researcher.
why: Culture, identity, language, and inclusive learning design.

claim: Students need AI competencies spanning a human-centered mindset, ethics, AI techniques/applications, and AI system design, progressing from understand to apply to create.
citation: UNESCO. AI Competency Framework for Students.
why: Student AI literacy, critical judgment, and co-creation.

claim: Teacher AI competency includes human-centered mindset, ethics, AI foundations, AI pedagogy, and AI for professional learning.
citation: UNESCO. AI Competency Framework for Teachers.
why: Teacher professional learning and responsible AI adoption.

claim: Evidence-based study design includes spacing, worked examples, combining graphics with verbal descriptions, and connecting abstract and concrete representations.
citation: Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning.
why: Practice structure, worked examples, representation, and durable learning.

claim: Autonomy, competence, and relatedness are central constructs for supporting self-determined motivation in educational settings.
citation: Niemiec, C. P., & Ryan, R. M. Autonomy, competence, and relatedness in the classroom: Applying self-determination theory to educational practice.
why: Motivation, learner agency, and challenge/support balance.

claim: A meta-analysis found small positive average effects of gamification on cognitive, motivational, and behavioral learning outcomes, with effects varying by design and context.
citation: Sailer, M., & Homner, L. The Gamification of Learning: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review.
why: Use gamification as a tested design mechanism, not as a proxy for pedagogy.
